layers.text: When you look at your reflection in the mirror, you see someone who looks like you, but isn't really you.

layers.title: እቲ ኣብ ውሽጢ ኣእምሮና ዝርአ ሓሶት

layers.text: Inadequate, unwanted, someone who always makes mistakes and is weaker than others.
Yet you accept it as your true identity.
Your brain is not showing you who you really are.
It is showing you a distorted image created by its internal lens.
Why do even capable, successful, or brilliant people see a broken, failure of a person when they look in the mirror?
The reason is that our brain shows us not the objective reality in the mirror, but the self-image it constructed from various life experiences.
Often when we hear "self-image," we think it only refers to the physical image of our face or body in the mirror.
But the psychological reality is quite different.
Self-image is the internal lens of your life imprinted in your mind.
Built since childhood from experiences of love, criticism, humiliation, or comparison, it is the internal picture through which you view yourself and your worth.
This internal lens does not show you reality as it truly is.
Instead, acting like an information filter, it filters out good things that contradict your internal picture, while highlighting negative evidence to confirm that picture in your mind.
This mental filter answers two fundamental life questions for us.
"Am I a capable person worthy of respect in front of others?" "Am I loved and accepted by people?" If the answer your mind gives is "NO", your self-image is negative and distorted.
Because by nature, every human being possesses competence and is worthy of being loved.
You might ask, "Then why do I constantly fail, make mistakes, and feel like people distance themselves from me?"

The reason is that you are living a self-fulfilling prophecy. Psychological studies confirm that people who believe "I am incompetent; I cannot do this" lose 35 to 40 percent of their cognitive efficiency and problem-solving capacity during testing.
Furthermore, individuals who believe "I am unlovable" exhibit 60 percent higher behavioral withdrawal compared to others.
This behavioral retreat is precisely what prevents them from forming deep friendships.
Incompetence and isolation are thoughts constructed by your mind, not your true nature.
Now, let's examine 5 major warning signs that indicate your self-image is distorted.

1. Harsh self-hatred and self-criticism: The Self-Hate Trap. When you make a minor mistake at work or in life, instead of saying "I'll learn from this mistake," does your mind say, "I am a total failure!
I am a worthless, terrible person!" and harshly criticize yourself?
Harsh self-hatred is a warning sign created when your mind views you as its own worst enemy, generating severe psychological distress.

2. The compulsive online comparison loop: When you pick up your phone and scroll through social media, seeing other people's successful lives or wealth, do you immediately feel feelings of inadequacy and weakness inside?

Researchers analyzing over 55,440 participants across 83 major studies confirmed that the more you compare yourself to others on social media, the higher your feelings of self-hate and body dissatisfaction become.
3. Excessive perfectionism: Do you trap yourself in endless work until exhaustion under the rule "If everything I do isn't flawless, I am a failure"?
Striving for perfectionism does not stem from a love for your work.
It is a protective shield your brain constructs out of fear that people will see your flaws and reject you.
4. Safety behaviors and social avoidance: Do you hide from social gatherings out of fear that people will criticize you?
When you hide from people, it feels like temporary relief.
But in reality, hiding makes you feel isolated, reinforcing the negative image that says "See, nobody wants you," creating the very isolation and distance you feared.
5. Rumination: Before falling asleep, do you replay minor mistakes you made yesterday or awkward moments in front of people over and over in your head?
This constant rumination continuously fuels our internal negative beliefs, keeping feelings of anxiety and embarrassment alive within us.
The image you hold of yourself is not your true identity.
It is merely a mental picture shaped by yesterday's fears and other people's criticisms.
እቲ ናይ ሓቂ መንነትካ (Who You Truly Are)
Now, when you look at yourself in the mirror or doubt your worth, remember this: "Perhaps... the way you see yourself is not who you truly are."
